BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) — The U.S. military formally transferred authority over Baghdad’s “Green Zone” to Iraqi control on Thursday, as new agreements governing the mission of international troops replaced a U.N. mandate.

An Iraqi honor guard paraded outside the former palace of Saddam Hussein in Baghdad on Thursday. Iraqi troops assumed control of checkpoints around the heavily protected district, formally known as the International Zone, which houses Iraqi government offices and the U.S. Embassy.

Saddam Hussein’s Republican Palace, which served as U.S. headquarters in Baghdad after the 2003 invasion that ousted Iraq’s longtime strongman, was among the facilities handed over during Thursday’s ceremony.

“This day is a great day in the history of the Iraqi people,” Iraqi military spokesman Maj. Gen. Qassim Atta said.

Maj. Gen. David Perkins, a U.S. military spokesman, underscored the significance of returning the former Republican Palace. “The palace was handed back to the Iraqi people, significant as a symbol of the head of the government and a sign of increased sovereignty,” he said at a news conference with Atta.

Thursday marked the first day of a U.S.-Iraqi pact allowing U.S. forces to remain in the country until 2011, though under tighter restrictions. Similar agreements have been signed with other coalition countries that continue to have forces in Iraq. A U.N. mandate authorizing international forces in the country expired Wednesday.

Perkins said American troops would continue to fight alongside Iraqi forces — “but the Iraqis will be in the lead.”

“When you come up to a checkpoint, the Iraqis will check your identification. They will make the decision if you come in or go out,” he said. “We will continue to be there to provide some technical capacity, to provide some mentoring, but you will see less and less American forces and more and more Iraqi forces — and they will have the majority of the responsibility for making those key decisions which determine the security of the capital.”

Iraq’s three-member Presidency Council ratified the new pact in December. Under the agreement, U.S. troops are to withdraw from Iraqi cities and towns by June 30, and all American troops are to leave the country by the end of 2011, more than eight years after the U.S.-led invasion that toppled Hussein.

The agreement authorizes the “temporary assistance” of U.S. forces but sharply limits their role. It requires Iraqi approval for all military operations and grants Iraqi courts the authority to try U.S. troops and contractors for “grave premeditated felonies.”

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) — On Thursday, the U.S. military officially transferred control of Baghdad’s heavily fortified “Green Zone” to Iraqi authorities, as new agreements regulating the role of foreign forces took effect in place of a United Nations mandate.

An Iraqi honor guard marched outside Saddam Hussein’s former palace in Baghdad during the ceremony. Iraqi soldiers assumed responsibility for checkpoints surrounding the secure district, officially called the International Zone, which contains Iraqi government offices as well as the U.S. Embassy.

Among the sites turned over was Saddam Hussein’s Republican Palace, which became the U.S. headquarters in Baghdad following the 2003 invasion that removed Iraq’s longtime ruler from power.

“This day is a great day in the history of the Iraqi people,” said Maj. Gen. Qassim Atta, a spokesman for the Iraqi military.

U.S. military spokesman Maj. Gen. David Perkins emphasized the symbolic importance of returning the former Republican Palace. Speaking at a news conference alongside Atta, he said the palace had been restored to the Iraqi people and described it as meaningful both as a symbol of government authority and as evidence of Iraq’s growing sovereignty.

Thursday was also the first day under a new U.S.-Iraq agreement permitting American forces to stay in Iraq until 2011, though under stricter limits. Comparable arrangements have been reached with other coalition nations that still have troops in the country. The previous U.N. authorization for international forces in Iraq expired on Wednesday.

Perkins said U.S. troops would keep fighting together with Iraqi forces, but he stressed that Iraqis would now take the leading role.

“When you come up to a checkpoint, the Iraqis will check your identification. They will make the decision if you come in or go out,” he said. He added that American forces would remain available to offer technical support and guidance, but that the public would increasingly see fewer U.S. troops and more Iraqi forces. Iraqis, he said, would hold most of the responsibility for major security decisions affecting the capital.

Iraq’s three-person Presidency Council approved the new agreement in December. According to its terms, U.S. forces must pull out of Iraqi cities and towns by June 30, and every American service member must leave Iraq by the end of 2011—more than eight years after the U.S.-led invasion that brought down Hussein.

The pact allows for the “temporary assistance” of U.S. troops, but it places major limits on what they can do. It requires Iraqi consent for all military operations and permits Iraqi courts to prosecute U.S. troops and contractors accused of “grave premeditated felonies.”

As part of the handover, Iraqi troops assumed control of checkpoints, entrances, and key facilities throughout the Green Zone. The district, long home to foreign embassies, Iraqi government offices, and U.S. military personnel, had been a central symbol of the American presence in Iraq since the 2003 invasion. Among the sites transferred to Iraqi authority was Saddam Hussein’s former Republican Palace, which had served as a major U.S. administrative and military hub after the fall of his regime.

Iraqi and U.S. officials described the transfer as an important symbol of Iraq’s growing sovereignty. For Iraqi leaders, taking control of the Green Zone represented a visible step toward reclaiming full authority over the country’s institutions and security. For the United States, the handover reflected a broader transition from direct control toward a supporting role.

The change came under a new U.S.-Iraqi security pact that permits American forces to remain in Iraq until 2011, but places them under tighter restrictions than before. Unlike the previous U.N. mandate, the new agreement gives the Iraqi government greater authority over military operations and the presence of foreign troops on its territory.

Although U.S. forces will continue to assist Iraqi troops with training, logistics, and security support, Iraqi forces are expected to take the lead in making security decisions. The handover of the Green Zone therefore served not only as a practical transfer of control, but also as a powerful sign of Iraq’s increasing responsibility for its own governance and national security.

**U.S. hands over control of Baghdad’s Green Zone to Iraqi authorities after U.N. mandate expires**

**BAGHDAD, Iraq** — The U.S. military has formally handed over control of Baghdad’s heavily fortified Green Zone to Iraqi authorities, marking a symbolic milestone in Iraq’s efforts to reclaim sovereignty after years of foreign military oversight.

The transfer came after the expiration of the United Nations mandate that had authorized the presence of U.S.-led multinational forces in Iraq. With that mandate ended, U.S. troops began operating under a bilateral security agreement negotiated between Washington and Baghdad, giving the Iraqi government greater authority over military operations and security arrangements inside the country.

The Green Zone, a sprawling enclave in central Baghdad that houses Iraqi government offices, foreign embassies and military facilities, became one of the most recognizable symbols of the U.S. presence in Iraq after the 2003 invasion. For years, access to the area was tightly controlled by U.S. and coalition forces amid frequent insurgent attacks and sectarian violence across the capital.

Iraqi officials described the handover as a major step toward restoring full national control.

“This is a day of sovereignty,” an Iraqi government official said, emphasizing that Iraqi security forces would now take the lead in managing checkpoints, access and protection inside the zone.

U.S. military officials said American forces would continue to support Iraqi troops when requested, but that the change reflected the growing role of Iraq’s army and police in securing the country.

The expiration of the U.N. mandate also signaled a broader shift in the legal framework governing the U.S. military presence in Iraq. Under the new security agreement, U.S. forces were required to withdraw from Iraqi cities and towns by mid-2009 and leave the country by the end of 2011, unless both governments agreed otherwise.

For many Iraqis, the Green Zone had long represented a divide between the country’s rulers and the daily hardships faced by ordinary citizens outside its blast walls. While security in Baghdad had improved significantly from the height of sectarian bloodshed, violence and political tensions remained a challenge.

The handover did not mean an immediate end to the American presence in the Green Zone, where the U.S. Embassy and military personnel continued to operate. But Iraqi forces assuming responsibility for the area underscored a changing balance of authority as Iraq moved into a new phase following years of war and occupation.

counterfactuals.output:
**BAGHDAD — Iraq assumes control of International Zone as new U.S. security pact takes effect**

**BAGHDAD, Jan. 1** — Iraq formally took authority Thursday over Baghdad’s heavily fortified International Zone, the seat of its government and the U.S. Embassy, in a symbolic transfer that coincided with the start of a new U.S.-Iraq security agreement redefining the American military presence in the country.

The area, long known as the Green Zone, has for years stood as the most visible symbol of foreign power in Iraq — a walled enclave of blast barriers, checkpoints and diplomatic compounds on the west bank of the Tigris River. Its handover to Iraqi control was presented by Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki’s government as a milestone in the restoration of sovereignty nearly six years after the U.S.-led invasion.

Iraqi soldiers and police assumed greater responsibility for gates, patrols and internal security arrangements in the zone, while U.S. forces remained present under the terms of the new security pact, which took effect at midnight.

“This is a historic day for Iraq,” an Iraqi military spokesman said in Baghdad. “The International Zone is now under the authority of the Iraqi government, and Iraqi forces are responsible for protecting the institutions of the state.”

The transfer came as the Status of Forces Agreement, approved by Iraq’s parliament in November, replaced the United Nations mandate that had authorized the U.S.-led coalition presence since 2003. Under the pact, U.S. forces must withdraw from Iraqi cities, towns and villages by the end of June 2009 and leave the country entirely by Dec. 31, 2011, unless a new agreement is negotiated.

The agreement also requires U.S. combat operations to be coordinated with Iraqi authorities and gives Baghdad expanded legal authority over certain crimes committed by U.S. personnel and contractors outside duty status.

A U.S. military spokesman described the change as part of a broader transition from coalition-led operations to Iraqi-led security.

“The agreement marks a new phase in our partnership with Iraq,” the spokesman said. “U.S. forces will continue to support Iraqi security forces, but the lead is increasingly Iraqi, and today’s transfer of the International Zone reflects that progress.”

The International Zone houses Iraq’s parliament, the prime minister’s office, key ministries and several foreign missions. For much of the war, access was tightly controlled by U.S. and coalition forces, and the area was viewed by many Iraqis as isolated from daily life in the capital. Insurgents frequently targeted it with rockets and mortars, even as violence across Baghdad declined sharply after the 2007 U.S. troop surge and the growth of Iraqi security forces.

Iraqi officials said the handover did not mean the area would immediately be opened to the public. Security restrictions were expected to remain in place, though Baghdad has said it intends gradually to reduce the zone’s footprint and restore normal traffic through parts of the capital.

“The International Zone will not become an open area overnight,” the Iraqi spokesman said. “But decisions about access and security will be Iraqi decisions.”

The new security pact is politically sensitive for both governments. In Iraq, supporters of Maliki say it establishes a clear timeline for the end of the U.S. military presence and restores national authority. Critics, including some Sunni and Shiite factions, have argued that it still grants Washington too much influence.

For the United States, the pact provides a legal basis for troops to remain in Iraq after the expiration of the U.N. mandate, while setting firm deadlines for withdrawal. U.S. commanders have said the timetable depends on continued improvements in Iraqi forces and on preventing a resurgence of insurgent groups.

Military officials on both sides emphasized that cooperation would continue.

“Our mission is not finished, but it has changed,” the U.S. spokesman said. “We will work by, with and through the Iraqi security forces.”

The handover of the Green Zone carried strong symbolism for a country still emerging from years of sectarian war, insurgent attacks and foreign occupation. Iraqi flags were raised over key checkpoints, and officials said the move represented a step toward normalizing government life in the capital.

For many Baghdad residents, however, the test will be practical rather than ceremonial: whether Iraqi forces can secure the capital without relying on American control, and whether the blast-wall city at Baghdad’s center can eventually be reintegrated into the life of Iraq’s capital.

For many Iraqis, the handover carried deep symbolism. The Republican Palace, with its grand halls and imposing architecture, had long represented the authority of Saddam Hussein’s rule. After his overthrow, it became one of the most visible symbols of the U.S. presence in Iraq. Its transfer to Iraqi control was presented by officials as evidence of the country’s growing sovereignty and the expanding role of Iraqi security forces.

“This is an important day for Iraq,” an Iraqi official said during the handover. “The responsibility for protecting our institutions and our capital is increasingly in Iraqi hands.”

U.S. commanders described the move as part of a broader shift away from direct control of Iraqi territory and facilities. Under security arrangements between Washington and Baghdad, Iraqi forces have been taking greater responsibility for urban security while American troops reduce their profile and reposition to supporting roles.

At the Green Zone checkpoints, Iraqi soldiers could be seen inspecting vehicles and checking identification, duties once largely performed or closely supervised by U.S. personnel. American forces remained nearby in an advisory capacity, but Iraqi commanders said their units were prepared to manage access to the enclave.

The Green Zone, located on the west bank of the Tigris River, has been one of the most protected areas in Iraq since the fall of Saddam. It has also been a frequent target for insurgent rocket and mortar attacks, making control of its entrances a sensitive security matter.

The transfer comes as Iraq continues to rebuild its institutions after years of war, sectarian violence and political instability. While violence has declined from the height of the conflict, concerns remain about the ability of Iraqi forces to prevent attacks and maintain order without extensive American support.

Still, Iraqi leaders portrayed the handover as a milestone.

“The palace belongs to the Iraqi people,” one official said. “Today it returns to them.”

For U.S. forces, the departure from the palace and checkpoints underscores the changing nature of the mission in Iraq. **BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN)** — A landmark security agreement between the United States and Iraq took effect Thursday, giving Iraqi authorities the lead role in the country’s security while allowing American troops to remain in Iraq until the end of 2011.

The pact, approved by Iraq’s parliament and signed by both governments late last year, replaces the United Nations mandate that had governed the presence of U.S.-led forces since the 2003 invasion.

Under the agreement, U.S. troops will gradually step back from combat operations and operate with greater Iraqi oversight. American forces are required to withdraw from Iraqi cities, towns and villages by the end of June 2009 and leave the country entirely by December 31, 2011, unless a new agreement is reached.

Iraqi officials hailed the start of the pact as a milestone in restoring national sovereignty after years of war, insurgency and sectarian violence.

“This is a historic day for Iraq,” a senior Iraqi official said, describing the agreement as a step toward full control over the country’s security and political future.

The agreement also gives Iraq more authority over U.S. military operations and requires coordination with the Iraqi government. It includes provisions governing the legal status of American troops and contractors, an issue that had been a source of intense debate among Iraqi lawmakers.

For U.S. commanders, the deal marks a new phase in the war, shifting the American mission toward training, support and advising Iraqi security forces. U.S. officials have said the timeline is designed to reflect improvements in Iraqi capabilities while ensuring the country does not slide back into widespread violence.

The agreement comes after a sharp reduction in violence from the height of the conflict, though bombings, political tensions and militant attacks remain a persistent threat.

More than five years after the U.S.-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein, the new arrangement sets the clearest timetable yet for the end of the American military presence in Iraq.

counterfactuals.output:
**Iraq Reclaims Green Zone as U.N. Mandate Ends and U.S. Withdrawal Timetable Begins**

**BAGHDAD —** Iraq formally regained control of Baghdad’s heavily fortified Green Zone on Thursday, marking one of the most visible symbols of the country’s restored sovereignty after years in which the district served as the nerve center of foreign authority and military power.

The transfer came as the United Nations mandate authorizing the presence of foreign troops in Iraq expired, ending the legal framework under which U.S.-led forces had operated since the 2003 invasion. In its place, a bilateral security agreement between Baghdad and Washington took effect, setting out a timetable for the withdrawal of American forces and placing new limits on U.S. military operations.

The Green Zone, a sprawling enclave on the west bank of the Tigris River, had long been the most protected area in Iraq. It housed the U.S. Embassy, Iraqi government offices, foreign missions, and military headquarters. For many Iraqis, it became a powerful symbol of occupation and separation — a walled-off seat of power insulated from the violence and hardships experienced elsewhere in the capital.

Iraqi officials hailed the handover as a milestone in the country’s postwar recovery and a sign that Baghdad was reclaiming authority over its own territory and security decisions.

“This day represents the return of sovereignty and the restoration of Iraq’s dignity,” Iraqi leaders said in statements marking the occasion. The Iraqi flag was raised at key points in the zone as responsibility for security shifted to Iraqi forces.

The end of the U.N. mandate represents a major legal and political turning point. Since 2003, multinational forces in Iraq had operated under Security Council authorization. With that mandate no longer in effect, foreign troops now require Iraqi approval to conduct operations, detain suspects, or move through the country.

Under the U.S.-Iraq security pact, often referred to as the Status of Forces Agreement, American troops must withdraw from Iraqi cities, towns, and villages by **June 30, 2009**. All U.S. forces are required to leave Iraq by **December 31, 2011**, unless a future agreement changes the arrangement.

The accord also gives Iraq greater jurisdiction over serious crimes committed by U.S. personnel while off duty and outside military bases, though implementation is expected to involve careful coordination between the two governments.

For Washington, the new agreement marks the beginning of a managed drawdown after more than five years of war. U.S. officials have described the timetable as conditions-based in practice but binding in its deadlines, saying American forces will increasingly shift from combat operations to training, advising, and supporting Iraqi security forces.

For Baghdad, the transition is both a political achievement and a test. Iraqi security forces will now shoulder greater responsibility at a time when violence has fallen sharply from the peak of sectarian warfare but insurgent attacks, bombings, and militia activity remain persistent threats.

The Green Zone handover also comes amid broader efforts by Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki’s government to assert state authority. Iraqi forces have taken a more prominent role in security operations across the country, and the government has sought to portray the new security framework as evidence that Iraq is no longer under foreign control.

Still, questions remain over whether Iraqi institutions are ready to manage the full burden of security. The country continues to face political divisions among Shiite, Sunni, and Kurdish factions, disputes over oil and territory, and the challenge of integrating or disbanding armed groups.

Many Iraqis greeted the change with cautious optimism. Some saw the reclaiming of the Green Zone as overdue, while others questioned whether sovereignty would be meaningful as long as tens of thousands of U.S. troops remained on Iraqi soil.

The U.S. Embassy and American military facilities will continue to operate within the zone, but under arrangements negotiated with the Iraqi government. Iraqi authorities are expected to gradually open parts of the area and expand access, though security concerns are likely to keep much of it restricted.

The developments mark one of the most consequential shifts in Iraq since the fall of Saddam Hussein. The expiration of the U.N. mandate, the return of the Green Zone to Iraqi control, and the start of the U.S. withdrawal timetable together signal the beginning of a new phase — one in which Iraq’s government will be judged increasingly by its ability to govern and secure the country on its own.
